 Karl Bushby: Leaving my son behind while I walked around the world was purely selfish
 Having embarked on his global trek with just $500, the adventurer is returning to Hull after 28 years and 31,000 miles. So what’s next?

 British adventurer and author Karl Bushby is expected to complete his ‘Goliath Expedition’ to walk from the southern tip of South America to his home city of Hull on Monday morning
 Credit : Geoff Pugh for the Telegraph
 Ed Cumming
 Show biography 
 Ed Cumming is a senior feature writer and columnist who started at the Telegraph in 2009, left in 2014 and came back in 2022 after a stint in the Left-wing press. His recent interviewees have included Jeremy Clarkson, Anna Wintour and Danny Dyer. He has never won a prize.
 Published 
 02 November 2026 6:01am GMT
 “‘Why?’ is probably the most commonly asked question,” says Karl Bushby . “It’s normally the first thing people say. It’s one of the most interesting questions. And there are all kinds of answers.”
 It is a bright blue autumn morning in Lincolnshire and Bushby, 57, is walking along the A153 in the shadow of the looming 15th-century red-brick walls of Tattershall Castle. In front of him, he is pushing a large trolley, a device he affectionately calls “The Beast”, on which his worldly possessions are loaded. About 50m or so behind him is his friend Angela Maxwell, 44, a fellow long-distance walker who has accompanied Bushby for long stretches of the past few years as he has traversed the globe (and who swam across the Caspian Sea with him in 2024). Bushby is bearishly fit, with shaggy blond hair and stubbly patches of grey in his beard, and he leads at a brisk pace: 5km per hour (about 3mph), whatever the weather, one step at a time.
 Writer Ed Cumming joins Bushby (and ‘The Beast’) on a stretch of the A153 in Lincolnshire as he makes the final push home
 This is what he has done, on and off, for the past 28 years. On October 5 1998, he set out from his mother’s home in Hull with a plane ticket to Patagonia, $500 and a simple mission: to get back without using any form of motorised transport. He left behind the Parachute Regiment (in which he had served), friends, family and an ex-wife with whom he had a young son in Northern Ireland. With them he also left behind a kind of normal life, in exchange for finding, in his words, “a way to get into the world”.
 Since then, whenever he has been able to, Bushby has woken up – sometimes in a tent by the side of the road, sometimes in a house or hotel – packed up The Beast, and worked out how to get himself 30km (18.6 miles) farther along his route. To pay for his food, equipment, occasional lodgings and other incidental expenses, Bushby has depended on corporate sponsorship as well as media deals, such as a two-hour documentary for National Geographic, The Walk Around the World , in 2015.
 All being well, on the morning of November 2 2026, Bushby will return to his 75-year-old mother’s home in Hull, after an official reception at the town hall. She will be there to greet him. After around 31,000 miles, 31 countries, punishing deserts, perilous swims, being held at gunpoint, illness, imprisonment and abandoned relationships, Bushby’s odyssey – one of the most extraordinary adventures in recent British history – will be at an end. He will have become the first person to complete an unbroken round-the-world walk.
 Bushby in Hull shortly before his departure for Patagonia on October 5 1998
 Credit : Ross Parry
 Although Bushby has enjoyed peaks of interest in his trip before, particularly in 2006 when he crossed the Bering Strait between the US and Russia, attention has been gathering ahead of Monday’s finale. On the road we are stopped several times by well-wishers, people who have followed his story, in some cases for decades. In the faces of everyone who stops to say “Well done” or pose for a selfie, you can see the same idea: they think about all the things they have done in their own life in the time Bushby has been on the road. “We were at primary school together,” says one woman, just beyond Tattershall Castle.
 His return will be a media circus, with interest from all over the world. Renowned film director Werner Herzog is making a documentary about him. (Bushby is a distinctly Herzogian figure.) There will be live shows, books and TV appearances. There is a family to reunite with, including his son, 36, and a 12-year-old granddaughter he has never met. Eventually, when the hullabaloo subsides, Bushby will have to work out what on earth to do with the rest of his life.
 “I’ll be 57, living with my mum, with no job,” he says, with a slight grimace, as he powers along the road. “The end has always felt so far away. Now all of a sudden it has felt like time has been compressed. It’s frightening. My life is like staring into a black hole right now.
 “Across this event horizon, I have no idea where I’m going to go. I sometimes think I have underestimated the psychological effect it is going to have on me. I need to be aware of it. The days are going to get a bit uncomfortable. Half of my life has been devoted to this single purpose which has defined my life. So that’s a little nerve-racking.”
 If he did not have one before, tens of thousands of miles and three decades on the road have given Bushby a philosophical streak. Dressed in a tattered khaki fleece, cheap jogging shorts and well-worn Merrell hiking shoes, he speaks with the reserved confidence of someone who has had to fend for himself for a long time.
 He is wryly funny. If nothing else, he has had plenty of time to reflect on how he has decided to live. A week or so before I accompany him on the road in Lincolnshire, we meet in Greenwich, where he has arrived after his cross-Channel swim.
 “When did they build that?” he asks, looking at a building he has evidently not seen in person before. “It used to be the Millennium Dome ,” I explain. “Ah yes,” he says, gesturing over the river towards the sparkling steel and glass of Canary Wharf. “This is all new to me.”
 Bushby was born in March 1969 into an Army family. His father, Keith, served in the SAS. His mother, Angela, worked in a confectionery factory. He has a younger brother, Adrian, who is also in the military. Bushby was diagnosed at 13 as dyslexic, and found school challenging. He left at 16 with no qualifications, and joined the Junior Parachute Company. It took him five attempts to pass the training, but eventually he was accepted.
 In the 1990s, in his early 20s, he was stationed in Northern Ireland, towards the tail end of the Troubles . He married a local woman, Angela (seemingly every woman in Bushby’s life is called Angela) and they had a son, Adam, but they divorced five years later when they were living in Hampshire. Angela and Adam went back to Belfast. At that time, service personnel could only visit Northern Ireland if they were on active duty, so Bushby was separated from his young son.
 Restless with work and life, and inspired by a birthday card from his father about SAS troopers wondering whether it was possible to walk from New York to London, Bushby started to make a plan. After a couple of years plotting his route with atlases and guide books, he set out. The journey – which he dubbed “the Goliath Expedition” – would begin at the southern tip of Chile and take him up through the Americas, across to Russia and through Asia, back up through Europe and home.
 “Day one, you’re standing there with 50,000km ahead of you,” Bushby recalls. “We had no idea how this was going to work, but just this almost delusional sense of confidence that we could do it.” He often speaks in the royal “we” – perhaps as a gesture of gratitude to the team of friends, family, supporters, sponsors and well-wishers who have kept him on the road for all this time – but Bushby set out alone. “Thanks to my time in the regiment, I knew I could handle the day-in, day-out stuff, and I was confident I could survive on the road once that money ran out. We knew we were going into survival mode, we knew we had to come out of Patagonia, into the mountains, into Chile to survive.”
 It took him two years to make his way up the west coast of South America. He crossed the treacherous jungle of the Darién Gap, where he had guns pulled on him; through Panama, where he was briefly imprisoned in February 2001 for entering without a visa; and on into Mexico, where he was again threatened at gunpoint; before he made it to the US. In a powerful indictment of the American diet, he managed to put on weight as he crossed the country, despite walking 30km a day pushing a 100lb trolley.
 “Just getting through Alaska was a serious ass-whooping, with plenty of ‘I’m going to die’ moments,” he says. “The Arctic and sub-Arctic feel like they are trying to kill you all the time.”
 Bushby admits he feared for his life at times due to the punishing conditions, particularly in Alaska
 By March 2006, eight years after beginning his walk, Bushby had reached the Bering Strait, the sea between Alaska and Russia, which is frozen in winter but perilous to cross. He and another adventurer, Dimitri Kieffer, dragged their supplies on sledges and walked across the sea ice, which was continuously moving.
 Gaps in the ice meant they occasionally needed to swim, too. Over two weeks, they covered a winding path of more than 150 miles to traverse the strait, which measures more than 50 miles as the crow flies, in what is believed to be the first such crossing in that direction without mechanical or motorised assistance.
 “The Bering Strait was one miracle after another,” Bushby says. “We had this Moses moment, where the conditions set themselves up to give us that chance.” Any joy was short-lived, however. When they arrived in Russia, they were immediately detained by the country’s security agency, the FSB , which said their crossing was unauthorised.
 “They wanted me to go to jail for five years,” he says. Help came from an unlikely source. Bushby’s local MP in Hull was John Prescott, while the governor of Chukotka, the remote eastern region, was a little-known entrepreneur by the name of Roman Abramovich. A few high-level phone calls later, and Bushby was free.
 “They put their heads together, made this annoying thing go away and we were free to carry on through Russia,” he says. “You couldn’t get away with that today.”
 The 2008 financial crisis, which meant his sponsorship dried up, set Bushby back several years, however, as did visa bans and the Covid pandemic. For months before his final swim across the English Channel, he was stymied by the French authorities : cross-Channel swims are only permitted from England to France, not the other way around. But Bushby says navigating these challenges was as much a part of his mission as the sun, rain and snow.
 “This is what an odyssey in the 21st century looks like,” he says. “Half of it is literally dealing with these bureaucratic geopolitical problems, not just the environmental hurdles. There are some times where the solution is just to wait. If you look at the financial crisis, the visa ban and the pandemic, those three cost me nine years, waiting or struggling to find a solution. People don’t realise that half the journey has been about overcoming these problems because we weren’t willing to compromise.”
 Part of the reason his journey is compelling, I suggest, is that it has been a way of life rather than mere adventure. His stubborn adherence to his own rules – no transport, and no returning home till he arrived on foot – has made his life difficult, but it also serves as a reminder that however flat it might look online, the world is a wild and enormous place.
 “Especially compared to that digital landscape we’re all plugged into, this is old school,” Bushby says. “It’s that raw human stuff that people need more of. Because people are people. You need dirty fingernails and bruised knees. It becomes sterile [otherwise]. Especially with kids today, where we wrap them up in cotton wool and protect them to the point where we lose something . Kids need to go out there and get beaten up now and again. Flesh and blood stuff is scary, but you do need it.”
 He has been on the road for so long that he routinely meets people who have followed his story since they were children. “In Kazakhstan, we met a couple of cyclists in the middle of nowhere,” he says. “One of them was saying he had heard on the radio the story about two guys crossing the Bering Strait, and that’s what inspired him to travel. He didn’t realise he was talking to me.”
 He has also found the world full of people willing to help. “I have a more positive view of humanity [than when I set out],” he says. “In every country I’ve been to, even those who are our ‘enemies’, I’ve had people help me on numerous occasions.” It has softened him politically , too. “I left the UK probably on the more conservative side,” he says. “But it has made me more liberal. My bet is on humanity. I think we’re going to be just fine.”
 Bushby’s epic mission may have boosted his faith in humanity, but it has come at a terrible cost to his own relationships. He had reconciled himself to missing his son’s childhood, but he had hoped he would be back by the time he was 20. By that measure, he is 16 years late.
 “There is a disconnect and distance with family that has to be overcome,” he says. “It’s an odd one. There’s guilt there. That cross gets heavier the more the years go by. But you wrap it up in that container that is the mission. It’s the job. The way I squared the circle with Adam was by thinking that by doing this maybe I’ll have more meaning in his life, more value doing what I’m doing.”
 As technology improved, it became easier to keep in touch with his family from afar. When he left, he only had a film camera. Today, he has a smartphone with which he can stay in touch with loved ones, conduct Zoom calls with journalists around the world, post updates to his social media accounts, or listen to Telegraph podcasts. (On the road, he is devoted to Ukraine and Iran: The Latest .)
 He had hoped Adam would come out to join him when he was an adult, but although they have met on the road, he admits it “has not happened the way I imagined it would”.
 Bushby had two significant relationships along the way, during which he stayed for years in one place, but both fell by the wayside because he would not compromise on his mission.
 “There was Catalina in Colombia, for seven years – I gave that everything – and three years with Rika, who’s Japanese but who I met in Mongolia,” Bushby says. “The pandemic killed that [relationship] off. That’s the tough stuff: relationships, family. Sticking by our guns has been incredibly difficult.”
 He says he knew the emotional risks before he set out. “We predicted we would fall in love and get burnt, but that it wasn’t going to slow us down,” he says. “We managed to punch our way through that. That’s what it has to take. That mindset is fundamentally important. There are so many reasons to quit. But if you have the mindset that there is no going home [until the end], you’re in. People speak about the mission as if I left a life to go and do something. But I didn’t. My life was with me on the road. There was nowhere to fall back to.”
 The journey was inevitably often lonely. (Bushby in Alaska in 2006)
 Credit : Press Association/TikTok
 He adds that people often speak to him enviously about the great freedom they suppose he has had.
 “But I’m not really [free],” he says. “You’re locked into something. There’s nothing outside of this. You don’t have the money or time to do anything. You can’t have a relationship.”
 Still, he acknowledges that it has been a self-centred mission. “It has been a purely selfish way to be,” he says. “All I’ve had to think about every goddamned day for 20 years is getting me fed, watered and moved 30km down the road. And other people will pay a price for that. People who love you, people who are important to you, they will pay an emotional price for that. Be careful what it is you celebrate and who your heroes are . If you look at the personal lives of people like Shackleton and Cook and the others, they were horrible husbands and fathers. Don’t go looking there.”
 After a couple of hours in Lincolnshire, Bushby, Maxwell and I stop for coffee at the Wayside café, Tattershall. The owner asks whether they have come far. “About 50,000km,” Bushby replies. He and Maxwell make an entertaining platonic pair. She is originally from Oregon and chatty, whereas he defaults to quiet. On the final leg through England, she has started helping to organise Bushby’s endless media schedule; they are planning to do some events together.
 Maxwell says she is “99-per-cent certain” he will not go walking again once he is home. “He’s planning to donate The Beast to a little museum and live out his days doing talks. Karl’s more committed to the mission; I’m more devoted to the adventure.”
 After the media frenzy of the coming week subsides, Bushby hopes to find work in science education.
 Friend Angela Maxwell has accompanied Bushby on several stretches of his trek over the past few years
 Credit : Guzelian/Roger Moody
 “Fifteen minutes of fame goes away pretty quick,” he says. “You’ve got to work out what you want to do next.
 “It feels we have lived life to the full,” he adds. “That, pretty much, was the plan. The sense of adventure has been satisfied. I remember talking to the press outside my mother’s place before I left about how I didn’t want to live with regret. For me it’s about death. We’re dying. You only have one life to live. What are you going to do?”
 More big questions. After 31,000 miles and 28 years, Karl Bushby is still hunting for answers, one step at a time.
